name: Ivan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Japanese manga and some mobile game text into English, mostly for two small publishers who pay per chapter. My day starts around ten: I run the chapter through an AI model with a glossary I built, then I spend hours fixing tone, sound effects and the way characters talk to each other. I've written little scripts that check names and honorifics stay consistent, which is the part I'm proudest of. The pay is low, and my Japanese is honestly not as good as the senior people's, so I lean on the tools more than they'd like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone in a small flat above a phone repair shop, and I've got maybe ten days of money saved, because I bought a better graphics card for running models locally. There's nothing like my work in this town; it's all online. I'm fine with that, I like being at my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good assistant and a bad translator, and that the hype was always silly. I'd post my glossary script on the translators' forum and say, here's what it's actually good for. People would argue about it in the replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with this one, mostly. The tools make me fast enough to compensate for my weaker Japanese. The only problem is ten days of savings and publishers who sometimes skip a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, but sell my glossary checker as a small tool for other translators, maybe five a month per user. I'd ask both publishers for a third series so one quiet month doesn't sink me. And I'd stop buying hardware for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relaxed, with a little worry about the bank account. Nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your Japanese isn't as good as the senior translators'. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Without the AI tools, I'd be a slow junior. With them, I'm a fast junior who's good at the boring checking. I'm working on the language at night with drama shows, but that takes years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides if you get the third series?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The editor at the bigger publisher, who's about my age and also uses AI a lot. If I show her the checker saves her time, she'll give me more. That's how I got the second series.

say: AI is a **good assistant** and a bad translator, and the hype was silly.
I'd post my **glossary script** on the forum to show what it's good for.
think: The tools make me **fast enough** to cover my weaker Japanese.
My only problem is **ten days** of savings and skipped months.
do: Sell his **glossary checker** to other translators for about five a month.
Ask both publishers for a **third series**.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with a little worry about the bank account.
S0.quote: Without the AI tools, I'd be a slow junior. With them, I'm a fast junior who's good at the boring checking.
fieldNote: He uses the tools to **cover a skill gap**, and admits it.
His side project, a **glossary checker**, shows an early-mover instinct.
His **thin savings** come from buying hardware, not hardship.

steps.text: Sell his glossary checker script to other translators monthly
Ask both manga publishers for a third series
Run every chapter through his own AI glossary pipeline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators who learn the tools will be fine and those who don't won't, which I know sounds harsh. I'd say publishers should still pay a fair rate for the human pass. Online I'd be the guy posting tutorials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my per-chapter rate drops, because the publisher sees the AI doing more. But the editors will need someone to run the whole pipeline for many series at once, and I'm already doing that for myself. My income might go down for a year and then up, if I get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch the bigger publisher to make me their localisation coordinator, running the AI and checking three or four freelancers' work. I'd keep selling the checker tool and add a paid version. If that doesn't happen, I'd look at moving to the city, where there are game studios with Japanese staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but awake. It's like a test I've been studying for without knowing the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be checking other freelancers' work. Some of them might lose work to your pipeline. How do you think about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I try not to think about it too much. If I don't build the AI pipeline, someone at a bigger company will, and then nobody here gets anything. I'd at least keep the freelancers I know on the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your rate drops for a year with ten days of savings, what happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd live on rice and instant noodles and maybe sell the graphics card I just bought. My parents would help with a month's rent if I asked, but I'd rather not. That's the risky bit of my plan.

Publishers should still pay a **fair rate** for the human pass.

feel: **Nervous but awake**, like a test with no date.

fieldNote: He expects a **one-year income dip** on ten days of savings.
He sidesteps the **ethics** of displacing freelancers with a market argument.
His plan carries real **risk**, and he names it.

steps.text: Pitch the bigger publisher to make him localisation coordinator
Launch a paid version of his glossary checker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the honest thing: tools-people like me don't survive this either. I'd tell people to get practical skills while they can. I wouldn't pretend I had a clever answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the pipeline I'm proud of becomes a button the publisher presses. My edge was being early, and in two years everyone is late. The only thing left is in-person work, and I don't have much of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any in-person interpreting I could get for the next three years, like hosting Japanese business visitors at factories in the region. I'd also learn phone and laptop repair from the man downstairs, because hands-on work lasts until about 2031. I'd sell the graphics card straight away to buy time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's strange to be so far ahead and still end up in the same place as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Phone repair from the man downstairs. Have you talked to him about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only joking, once, when I dropped my phone. But he's been asking if I know anyone who can help on Saturdays. I'd go down and ask him properly the week AGI was announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that I'm switching to something with my hands for a while, like my grandfather who fixed radios. They'd be relieved, actually. They never really understood what I did.

fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** for hands-on repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning for people who use it. I'd tell other translators to build something now that pays them later. I'd try to sound useful, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three good years running AI localisation, maybe the best of my career. Then it ends around 2030 or 2031. The trick is to turn those years into money and a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the coordinator role and save hard, aiming for three months of money by 2029. I'd sell the checker to as many translators as possible while it's still worth something. And I'd start learning electronics repair in the evenings, because hands-on work lasts until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd be busy, and busy suits me. I don't do well sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about saving hard. Have you ever saved before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I always spend it on hardware. I'd have to set up an automatic transfer and give my cousin the password, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the five years you'd enjoy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The building part. Running a team of tools and people across five series would be the most fun I've had at work. The fun just has an end date.

fieldNote: He sees a **short boom** and plans to bank it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should treat it as a career change window. I'd post a plan for translators: use the tools, save, learn a second trade. I'd sound fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do well for several years, and by 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with savings and a second skill. That's a decent position. I'm the type who moves early, so time helps me more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the localisation side properly, maybe start a tiny agency with two other translators by 2028. I'd put a fixed amount aside every month and invest a bit in a simple index fund. Around 2032 I'd start moving towards repair or technical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with some unease about the bigger world. I'd worry more about my friends than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your friends more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because most of my translator friends don't use the tools and say they never will. I'd be telling them every year, and they'd keep saying later. I can't make them move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a tiny agency. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three of us, one shared pipeline, maybe ten series. We'd sell speed and quality to small publishers. We'd close our tiny agency cheerfully in about 2034, before it closes us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because being early stops mattering and I'd have ten days of money. What would help is short, paid courses in hands-on trades, open to freelancers, not only people with contracts. I'd sign up the first day.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd do if AI plateaus right after I sell the graphics card. That would be the most annoying outcome. I'd be the translator who sold my tools a month before they mattered.

headlineQuote: I'd be the translator who sold my tools a month before they mattered.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** Japanese–English manga and game translator who uses AI every day.
He lives alone above a phone repair shop with about **ten days** of savings, spent on hardware.
He covers his weaker Japanese with **self-built tools** and wants to run AI pipelines.
Pragmatic, he blames no one and argues that if he doesn't build it, **someone bigger** will.
He swings from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, then back to uneasy with a decade to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when being early stops mattering and he has ten days of money.
whatWouldHelp: Short, **paid courses** in hands-on trades that freelancers can join.
